node.date_label: The Monied Metropolis (2001) · Empire of Cotton (2014) · with Seth Rockman, Slavery’s Capitalism (2016) · interviews (2019, 2020) · Capitalism (2025, metadata only)
node.description: Studies the social and political making of capitalism across urban and global scales. The Monied Metropolis asks how New York’s divided capital-owning elites formed a coherent bourgeoisie through institutions, culture and political conflict. Empire of Cotton’s “war capitalism” stresses the connections among armed trade, land expropriation, enslavement and state power. His later first-person explanations advocate tracing relations among different regions and forms of labour rather than assuming one Western path. These are attributed historical arguments: Hilt questions parts of the industrialisation explanation, while Burnard and Riello contest the chronology and emphasis of the new history of capitalism. The existing debate entry retains those disagreements in detail.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Monied Metropolis: New York City and the Consolidation of the American Bourgeoisie, 1850–1896 (2001; introduction pp. 1–9 read); Empire of Cotton: A Global History (2014; existing authorised excerpt and later author interviews); with Seth Rockman, eds., Slavery’s Capitalism: A New History of American Economic Development (2016; joint editorial credit checked, collection unread); LSE interview with Tom Wilkinson (2019) and Harvard GrowthPolicy interview with Devjani Roy (2020), selected methodological answers; Capitalism (Penguin Press, 2025; publication metadata only).
node.scope_note: Promotes the existing roster identity sven_beckert without replacing its identity note or assigning external identifiers, life dates or a career interval. Fresh substantive reading comprises Monied Metropolis introduction pp. 1–9 and the author’s 2019/2020 interview answers; original archives, full books, the Slavery’s Capitalism introduction and Capitalism (2025) remain unread. Criticism uses the existing partial-source witnesses: Hilt pp. 516–517 and Burnard/Riello abstract and selected pages, with their recorded reading limits unchanged. Hilt’s doubts about mechanisms and Burnard/Riello’s global/Atlantic critique remain distinct; Baptist-specific torture/productivity charges are not attributed to Beckert. The three relationships record contributions, not proven transmission to every practitioner, a field origin or consensus. Later publication facts do not extend any field’s review boundary.

proposed_edges.map_label: Urban institutions and bourgeois class formation
proposed_edges.relationship: Reconstructs how New York’s divided capital-owning elites became a more coherent bourgeoisie through institutions, cultural practices and political conflict (The Monied Metropolis, 2001).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author’s introduction pp. 2–3 and 6–9 read. Shared wealth does not automatically explain common identity or political power; class formation is the historical problem. This contribution brings elite formation into urban/social history without claiming Beckert founded the field or that the complete book’s cases have been independently verified.

proposed_edges.map_label: War capitalism: violence, land, labour and states
proposed_edges.relationship: Contributes “war capitalism” as an account of the violent trading, land and labour arrangements from which industrial capitalism developed (Empire of Cotton, 2014; author’s explanation, 2019).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The authorised excerpt remains the existing limited book witness; Beckert’s LSE answer on the term was freshly read. His historical claim about links among armed trade, dispossession, enslavement and state power is attributed, not accepted as a settled causal explanation of industrialisation. The existing Hilt and Burnard/Riello partial readings and the new_history_of_capitalism strand retain their criticisms. Baptist-specific productivity claims are not assigned to Beckert.

proposed_edges.relationship: Explains a global method that relates merchants, plantations and manufacturing across regions, treating capitalism as connected diversity rather than a single preordained path (GrowthPolicy interview, 2020).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Beckert’s second answer was read: comparative regional sites and linked labour regimes support this account of his method. A first-person research strategy does not establish universal adoption, prove every regional empirical claim, or derive a new argument from the unread 2025 book. The field’s prior approaches, Benton addition and review boundary remain intact.
